title: Sixteen blind and low-vision adults use Eyevisor in a two-week diary study; researchers analyze 316 entries after exclusions
summary: Sixteen blind and low-vision adults submitted 354 entries using Eyevisor, built on Azure AI Vision. Researchers analyzed 316 entries after exclusions; satisfaction averaged 2.76 out of 5.
account: Ricardo Gonzalez Penuela, Jazmin Collins, Cynthia Bennett and Shiri Azenkot (Cornell Tech and Google) ran a two-week diary study. It had 16 blind and low-vision adults in the United States (five men, 11 women, aged 24 to 67). Recruitment was via National Federation of the Blind mailing lists. They used an iPhone scene-description app the researchers built on Microsoft's Azure AI Vision image description application programming interface (API). It was chosen because it “exposes the latest deep learning algorithms”. Seeing AI also uses it. Participants submitted 354 entries (13 to 39 each). Researchers excluded 22 because of technical failures and 16 setup entries, leaving 316 for analysis. Figure 2 labels the application Eyevisor. Documented uses include P1 photographing glasses. She “was not sure if this was my husband's sunglasses or my old pair of reading glasses from 4 years ago”. She got an answer without calling him. P5 photographed a hotel bed to check his roommate was not in it, and P15 photographed wine bottles in a shop rather than touching them. Participants scored descriptions 2.76 out of 5 for satisfaction and 2.43 out of 4 for trust on average. The authors say satisfaction did not track accuracy because users inferred information from partially correct descriptions. The paper appeared at CHI 2024 (doi 10.1145/3613904.3642211). The arXiv version was submitted on 22 March 2024. The study dates are not reported. The CHI EA 2025 follow-up used a custom app, VisionPal, and documented failures such as hallucinated braille labels.
purpose: The study app was built to describe photographed scenes for blind and low-vision users, emulating Seeing AI's scene channel. The documented identifications were that purpose.
system: Cornell Tech scene-description study app, labeled Eyevisor in Figure 2, using Microsoft Azure AI Vision’s image-description API.
developer: Cornell Tech (app); Microsoft (Azure AI Vision image description API)
deployer: Study participants (16 blind and low-vision adults)

ratings.reason: Participants completed small daily identifications without asking family. They rated descriptions 2.76/5 for satisfaction and 2.43/4 for trust on average. The app could not read text.

ai_role.statement: Azure AI Vision generated every description. The researchers' app only submitted photos and collected ratings. The paper documents individual successful uses and an overall judgment that descriptions “still need significant improvements”. Participants were allowed to use other tools during the study, so the diary covers only what they chose to photograph with this app.

echoes.setting: Follow-up two-week diary study with 20 BLV people using an MLLM-enabled visual-interpretation app the authors developed (VisionPal per an earlier check); 553 entries, preliminary analysis of 60 from six participants: trust 3.75/5, satisfaction 4.15/5, with trust in high-stakes uses such as medical dosage advice (CHI EA 2025, arXiv 2503.05899)

comparator.after: She was happy to get an answer without having to call her husband.
comparator.quote: For example, P1 submitted a photo of a pair of sunglasses when she “was not sure if this was my husband’s sunglasses or my old pair of reading glasses from 4 years ago.” She was happy to get an answer without having to call her husband.

later.note: The same Cornell Tech group's follow-up two-week diary study (CHI EA 2025), with 20 BLV people using a newer app they built on a multimodal large language model, collected 553 entries; a preliminary analysis of 60 entries found trust 3.75/5 and satisfaction 4.15/5, higher than the 2024 scores.
later.quote: We found that participants considered the application's visual interpretations trustworthy (mean 3.75 out of 5) and satisfying (mean 4.15 out of 5).

fields.account: Ricardo Gonzalez Penuela, Jazmin Collins, Cynthia Bennett and Shiri Azenkot (Cornell Tech and Google) ran a two-week diary study. It had 16 blind and low-vision adults in the United States (five men, 11 women, aged 24 to 67). Recruitment was via National Federation of the Blind mailing lists. They used an iPhone scene-description app the researchers built on Microsoft's Azure AI Vision image description application programming interface (API). It was chosen because it “exposes the latest deep learning algorithms”. Seeing AI also uses it. Participants submitted 354 entries (13 to 39 each). Researchers excluded 22 because of technical failures and 16 setup entries, leaving 316 for analysis. Figure 2 labels the application Eyevisor. Documented uses include P1 photographing glasses. She “was not sure if this was my husband's sunglasses or my old pair of reading glasses from 4 years ago”. She got an answer without calling him. P5 photographed a hotel bed to check his roommate was not in it, and P15 photographed wine bottles in a shop rather than touching them. Participants scored descriptions 2.76 out of 5 for satisfaction and 2.43 out of 4 for trust on average. The authors say satisfaction did not track accuracy because users inferred information from partially correct descriptions. The paper appeared at CHI 2024 (doi 10.1145/3613904.3642211). The arXiv version was submitted on 22 March 2024. The study dates are not reported. The CHI EA 2025 follow-up used a custom app, VisionPal, and documented failures such as hallucinated braille labels.
